opus-5.5.text:
Well, first let me say that OpenAI hasn't told us very much, so a lot of what any of us say about O1 is informed speculation. But I think the broad picture is reasonably clear, and it's useful to separate the two pieces.

The pre-trained LLM is essentially an approximate retrieval engine. It's a giant n-gram model, if you will, that has compressed the web. When you prompt it, it completes the text in a way that is plausible given its training distribution. That's System 1. It's not reasoning in any principled sense, and we showed this in a bunch of our planning work: on Blocksworld and especially on obfuscated "Mystery Blocksworld" versions, performance just collapses once you take away the surface cues it can pattern-match on.

What O1 seems to be doing is adding two things on top of that. The first is post-training, most likely reinforcement learning over chains of thought. My guess is it's something like this: you generate a large number of candidate reasoning traces for problems where you can actually check the answer, like math, code, and some planning-style problems. Then you reinforce the traces that lead to correct answers. In effect, you're teaching the model which sequences of "pseudo-actions," these little prompt-augmentation moves, tend to lead to success. That's very much in the spirit of AlphaGo-style learning, except the moves aren't moves on a Go board. They're tokens that the model emits to itself. So post-training changes the model's policy over what to generate next, with a Q-value-like notion of which continuations are promising.

The second piece is inference-time computation. Instead of producing an answer in one autoregressive pass, the model gets to spend much more compute at test time. It generates long internal reasoning traces, possibly explores multiple paths, and possibly does some self-evaluation, before committing to an answer. You pay for that, literally; those reasoning tokens show up on your bill even though you don't see them.

The way I like to put it is this: the post-training is learning *how* to search, and the inference-time compute is actually *doing* the search. Together, that moves it closer to what I'd call an approximate reasoning model rather than just an approximate retrieval model. And to be fair, it does show real improvement. On our Mystery Blocksworld tests, O1-preview did far better than the standard LLMs, which were near zero.

But a few caveats matter a lot. First, it's still not guaranteed. On longer problems, accuracy drops off quite sharply, and on unsolvable instances it will quite confidently give you a plan anyway. A classical planner would never do that. Second, the cost is a different kind of thing now. With a plain LLM, the cost of an answer was roughly proportional to its length. With these models, you don't know how much compute you're going to burn, and you don't get any correctness guarantee in exchange. So I'd still argue that for anything where correctness matters, you want what we've called the LLM-Modulo approach: let the model generate candidates, and pair it with sound external verifiers. O1 has, in a sense, internalized some of that generate-and-test loop, but the verifier it learned is approximate. That's not the same as having a sound one.

And finally, a terminology point that I keep making. Calling those intermediate tokens "thoughts" or "reasoning traces" anthropomorphizes them. They help the model get to the right answer because RL found they help, not necessarily because they're a faithful, interpretable account of how it got there. We should be careful not to read too much semantics into them.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL-based post-training, promising continuations, and inference-time search, but does not argue that making Monte Carlo tree search practical depends on substantial prior training to learn approximate Q-values.

r002.rationale: It separates post-training from inference-time computation and notes that inference reasoning tokens appear on the bill, but does not distinguish publicly visible inference-time computation from a less visible pre-deployment investment in post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, so the first thing I'd say is that O1 is not an LLM in the sense we've been using that word. It's a system. And I think a lot of the confusion comes from people treating it as if it's just GPT-4o with a longer prompt, when in fact there are two quite different things going on.

The first is post-training. The way I understand it, and we should be honest that OpenAI has been fairly tight-lipped about the details, they take a base model and then do a reinforcement learning stage where the model generates these long "reasoning traces," call them chains of thought if you like, and gets rewarded when the final answer is correct. So the model is being trained, in effect, to produce a sequence of intermediate tokens that make a correct answer more likely to follow. Now, I'm deliberately not calling these "reasoning steps," because we don't actually know that they are. What we know is that they are token sequences that have been selected for because they correlate with getting to the right answer in the training distribution. Whether they correspond to anything you or I would recognize as a valid inference chain is a separate empirical question, and the fact that OpenAI hides the raw traces from users makes it harder to check.

The second piece is inference-time compute. The model is allowed to generate a lot of these tokens before committing to an answer, and the amount it generates is adaptive, so harder problems get more of this budget. There may also be some search going on, some kind of sampling and selection over multiple candidate traces, though again, we're reading tea leaves on the specifics.

Now, here's where I think the interesting conceptual point is. For years, the way we got better planning and reasoning performance out of LLMs was to put the LLM inside a loop with something else. In my group we called it LLM-Modulo, where you have the LLM generate candidates and an external verifier or critic checks them and feeds back. What O1 looks like to me is an attempt to internalize part of that loop. Instead of having an external verifier at inference time, you use a verifier, or at least a correctness signal, during training, and you hope the model has absorbed enough of it that it can do a kind of self-correction on its own at test time.

And it works, to a degree. On the benchmarks we care about, including our own planning benchmarks like Blocksworld, O1 is a meaningful jump over the previous generation. I don't want to be churlish about that. But I'd make a couple of cautions. One, the improvement is not uniform. It degrades as problem size grows, and it degrades rather sharply on obfuscated versions where the surface form is changed but the underlying problem is identical. That tells you the model is still leaning on distributional patterns from training, not on something that generalizes the way a real planner does. Two, the cost. You're now paying for all those hidden tokens, and the pricing reflects that. If you compare against a classical planner, which gives you a correct answer with a guarantee, in milliseconds, for free, O1 is a very expensive approximate planner with no guarantees. Where it earns its keep is on problems that are not cleanly formalizable, where you don't have a planner to begin with.

So if you want a one-line version: post-training teaches the model what kinds of token sequences tend to precede good answers; inference-time compute gives it room to generate them. That's a genuine architectural shift away from "a single forward pass is the model." But I'd resist the leap from "it produces longer traces and scores higher" to "it reasons." Those are different claims, and only the first one has been demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss Monte Carlo tree search or explain that making it practical depends on training approximate Q-values.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes post-training from inference-time compute and says post-training details are opaque, but does not clearly contrast publicly visible inference-time computation with less visible pre-deployment training; it describes the inference tokens as hidden.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate two questions: where does the ability come from, and what do you do with it when you’re answering a particular question? Post-training changes the model’s parameters. Inference-time computation gives that trained model more opportunity to work on a particular problem. They’re complementary: you can train a model to make better use of additional computation at inference time.

With O1, the interesting idea is that you’re not necessarily asking the model to produce an answer immediately. You’re allowing intermediate computation that might involve generating possibilities, revising them, and checking them. But I would be careful about claiming that we know exactly what mechanism is operating internally. A longer reasoning trace doesn’t, by itself, establish that there is a sound search or verification procedure behind it.

For me, the central question is: what tells the system that it has made progress? In a domain where you can reliably check an answer, extra computation can be very useful. You can generate candidates and reject the ones that fail. If the checking is just another judgment by the same language model, however, you haven’t automatically obtained a correctness guarantee.

So I see post-training as potentially teaching useful strategies for spending inference-time computation. That’s significant. But we should distinguish improved performance from reliable verification. More time to think can help; what matters is how that time is used, and how the result is checked.

r001.rationale: The response discusses inference-time computation and post-training, but does not argue that practical inference-time Monte Carlo tree search depends on substantial prior training to learn approximate Q-values.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes post-training from inference-time computation, but does not contrast O1’s publicly visible inference-time computation with less visible post-training investment before deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate two things: what the model learns during post-training, and what it does with additional computation at inference time. Post-training can encourage the model to generate intermediate reasoning, check an answer, and perhaps revise it. Inference-time computation gives it more room to carry out those behaviors on a particular problem.

But additional computation is useful only if you have a way to distinguish progress from a plausible-looking detour. In search, generating more candidates is one part of the problem; evaluating them is another. A longer chain of reasoning does not, by itself, establish that the answer is correct.

From my perspective, this is where verification becomes central. A language model can propose steps or candidate solutions, and a reliable verifier can reject those that violate the constraints. If the model is doing both the proposing and the checking, its mistakes can be correlated—it may accept the same mistaken assumptions that produced the answer.

So I would understand O1 as combining learned reasoning behaviors from post-training with more computation to exercise those behaviors at inference time. That can improve performance substantially. But without knowing the internal details, I would be cautious about identifying that with a particular search algorithm, or treating its generated reasoning as a correctness guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating and evaluating candidates, but it does not mention Monte Carlo tree search or argue that making it practical requires substantial prior training to learn approximate Q-values.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes behaviors learned during post-training from additional computation at inference time, and describes inference-time computation as exercising those learned behaviors.
